4.5a — The Full State Machine: Back to Patrol

Everything you built this unit is one animal: a machine with states, transitions, and no memory it does not need. Today you draw it, trace it, and connect it to the biggest idea in the AP exam's algorithms unit: selection decides everything.

Concept Lab ~20 min

You have written every line of this enemy already. Read the whole Update path at once and count the behaviors: 

private void Update()
{
    if (isPlatformer)
    {
        PlatformerMove();   // STATE: PATROL
    }
    else
    {
        TopDownMove();      // STATE: PATROL (when far) or CHASE (when near)
    }
}

Inside TopDownMove the chase is an if; outside it, the attack is a collision handler with a cooldown. Now draw the machine on paper — states as boxes, transitions as labeled arrows:

FromEvent / conditionTo
PATROLdistance to player < chaseDistanceCHASE
CHASEevery frame: move toward player (normalized)(stay in CHASE)
CHASEcontact (collision)ATTACK (deals damage on cooldown)
CHASEdistance >= chaseDistancePATROL

The fourth row is the one the teacher's design asks about: "returns to patrol when the player flees." Find it in the code — there is no explicit "return to patrol" line. The chase is inside an if; when the if stops matching, the enemy simply falls back to doing nothing extra. The patrol was never switched off, it was just outvoted. The most elegant state machines hide exits inside conditions.

Socratic

The AP exam says an algorithm needs sequencing, selection, and iteration. Label all three in the enemy's code: where is sequence, where is selection, and where is iteration? (The iteration one is sneaky — think about what calls Update.)

Build Lab ~25 min

Step 1 — prove the diagram with Debug.Log. Instrument TopDownMove for five minutes (then delete it):

if (dist < chaseDistance)
{
    Debug.Log("CHASE");
    ...
}
else
{
    Debug.Log("PATROL");  // you will have to make the else explicit
}

Walk the boundary in and out: the Console flickers CHASE/PATROL/CHASE. You are watching state transitions print in real time. Why is "flickering at the edge" not a bug — and which number (chaseDistance) would you tune to make the flicker stop?

Step 2 — the ATTACK column is a lie (mostly). Notice: attack is not a state in the code, it is a collision event that can fire during CHASE or even during PATROL (walk into a patrolling enemy!). Your diagram probably drew it as a state anyway — because that is how it FEELS. Designers draw the machine from the player's point of view; the code just makes the arrows cheap. Bosses in Unit 8 will have real phase states — this enemy fakes them.

Step 3 — name the states out loud. Write the three names — PATROL, CHASE, ATTACK — as comments next to the code lines that implement them. The comment IS the design document; the code is one implementation of it.

Bug Hunt: Break the machine

  1. Swap the chaseDistance and patrolDistance values (5 and 3). Which behavior gets weird first — and does the diagram still hold?
  2. Make isPlatformer true in the Overworld. Which states vanish — and what does that say about the enemy's whole brain in the cave scenes?
  3. Add a second chase if INSIDE the first: chase when dist < 5 AND dist > 2. What did you just invent (a dead zone!) — and where does the enemy stand when the player stands still inside it?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Design a fourth state

  1. Invent FLEE: the enemy runs AWAY when you get within 1.5 (a cowardly guard). Which subtraction flips, and where does the new arrow go on your diagram?
  2. Invent ENRAGE: after taking a hit (someday), double speed for 3 seconds. What field counts the 3 seconds — and which pattern does it borrow?
  3. Commit + push: "4.5a: state diagram + states named" — include a photo or ASCII of your diagram in the repo.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Draw the enemy's state machine from memory, with conditions on the arrows
  • Find "return to patrol" in the code — as the absence of a match
  • Label sequencing, selection, and iteration in real code
  • Explain why a drawn state and a coded state are different things
